periods.analysis: At-berth shore power utilization landed at 47.3%, a yellow baseline below our 60% target but high enough to show the system is being used where the operating conditions line up. Dana Okonkwo would call this a working-port number: not where Harborview needs it, but not a mystery either. The strongest plug-in performance came from compatible container calls at Berths 4 and 5, while Pier 2 cruise turnarounds and several breakbulk vessels still relied on auxiliary engines because cable-reach and vessel-readiness did not match the berth plan. The watch-item is the gap between scheduled eligible calls and actual energized hours, especially during afternoon cargo peaks when terminal electricians are also covering reefer-yard demand.
periods.recommendations: Create a weekly eligible-call reconciliation led by Seaport Operations, terminal electricians, and the harbor master so every missed plug-in has a named cause and owner. Prioritize cable-positioning fixes at Pier 2 and Berth 5 using the September vessel call sheet, and keep the green shoots alive by locking shore-power assignments into the berth plan at least 72 hours before arrival. Report the missed-energization log alongside fuel and emissions estimates so the yellow status is managed in operating terms, not just percentages.

periods.analysis: Utilization slipped to 45.7%, down 1.6 points from 47.3%, keeping the measure yellow and reminding us that winter reliability is part of sustainability. The decline was tied to two avoidable operational frictions: transformer T-4 inspections at the South Terminal and three late berth swaps that put shore-power-capable vessels on non-equipped faces. Holiday cargo surges also loaded the schedule toward short-dwell vessels, which are harder to connect before sailing windows close. The watch-item is berth discipline, because Harborview cannot buy its way to 60% if eligible ships are not consistently placed where the plugs are.
periods.recommendations: Freeze shore-power-capable berth assignments after the 48-hour operations call unless the Deputy Port Director approves a documented exception. Add a winter maintenance window for vaults SP-2A, SP-4C, and SP-5B before the next peak shipping week, with contingency generators explicitly not counted as shore power. Continue the weekly reconciliation from Q3 and publish a simple terminal-by-terminal miss code so operators see exactly where the 1.6-point loss came from.

periods.analysis: The measure improved to 48.5%, up 2.8 points from 45.7%, still yellow but moving in the right direction after the Q4 reset. The rebound came from better pre-arrival confirmation with OceanBridge, Pacific RoRo, and the cruise agents, plus fewer last-minute berth swaps during the January and February schedules. Crews also shortened average connection time on Berth 4 by staging the high-voltage cable cart before line handling was complete, a small operating change with a real utilization payoff. The watch-item remains vessel compatibility documentation, because several captains arrived with incomplete load certificates and lost the first hour of potential energized time.
periods.recommendations: Make pre-arrival shore-power readiness a mandatory field in the PortCall Harborview system, with missing certificates flagged 24 hours before pilot boarding. Extend the Berth 4 cable-cart staging practice to Berths 3 and 5 and track connection minutes as a leading indicator, not just final utilization. Hold the yellow line by pairing every new carrier service agreement with a shore-power onboarding checklist reviewed by Environmental Programs and Marine Operations.

periods.analysis: Utilization edged up to 49.2%, a 0.7-point gain from 48.5%, which is steady progress but still yellow against the 60% target. The spring cruise season helped by bringing more compatible calls, yet that benefit was partly offset by construction fencing near Pier 2 during the apron resurfacing project. Harborview’s port is busy, growing, and financially strong, but growth adds choreography: more boxes, more passengers, and less tolerance for a cable cart parked in the wrong lane. The watch-item is construction-interface control, particularly whether Pier 2 access restrictions continue to suppress otherwise eligible plug-ins.
periods.recommendations: Require the apron contractor and Seaport Operations to review shore-power access at the daily 0600 coordination huddle until Pier 2 lanes are fully restored. Sustain the Q1 readiness gains by keeping certificate checks in PortCall Harborview and adding a same-day text alert to terminal electrical supervisors when an eligible vessel is inbound. Prepare a Q3 berth-access map that protects cable-cart travel paths during cruise days and high-volume container gates.

periods.analysis: Utilization fell to 47.6%, down 1.6 points from 49.2%, so the measure remains yellow with a clear summer operations warning. Heat, cruise passenger volume, and peak refrigerated cargo all competed for electrical crew attention, and the port lost plug-in hours during three tight-turn calls at Pier 2 and one late container shift at Berth 5. This is not a capacity-crisis story, but it is a coordination story: the hardware exists, the eligible calls exist, and the operating window is too often being spent on set-up. The watch-item is peak-day staffing coverage, especially Fridays and Sundays when cruise, reefer, and gate operations stack up.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a July-September Shore Power Peak Desk on Fridays and Sundays with one dispatcher, one terminal electrician lead, and Marine Operations on the same radio channel. Pre-stage a second cable-handling crew for Pier 2 cruise turns and measure whether it recovers at least the lost 1.6 points next quarter. Keep the successful berth-readiness checklist, but add a red-flag rule that any eligible vessel with less than six hours dwell gets a connection plan before the pilot boards.

periods.analysis: Utilization declined again to 45.8%, down 1.8 points from 47.6%, which keeps us yellow and pushes the trend uncomfortably close to the lower edge of acceptable performance. The main drag was not demand; it was execution around weather, holiday congestion, and two shore-power cabinet faults at SP-3B that took eligible hours off the table. Dana’s read is direct: Harborview’s gateway economy is strong, but the grid-to-ship handoff has to be treated like a core service, not an environmental add-on. The watch-item is asset reliability, with SP-3B and the South Terminal cable reels now needing tighter preventive maintenance before the winter pattern repeats.
periods.recommendations: Move SP-3B into a 30-day corrective maintenance sprint with Facilities, the shore-power vendor, and terminal electricians documenting root cause, parts lead time, and return-to-service testing. Add spare connector kits and reel brake assemblies to the port storeroom before the next holiday surge. Continue the Peak Desk concept on weather-event days, and require a post-call review for every eligible vessel that leaves without connecting.

periods.analysis: Utilization recovered to 48.7%, up 2.9 points from 45.8%, a welcome correction that still leaves the measure yellow and short of the 60% standard. The SP-3B maintenance sprint restored lost availability, and the January carrier meetings produced cleaner readiness declarations before arrival. We also saw better discipline from the South Terminal berth desk, with fewer eligible vessels moved away from powered berths after the 48-hour lock. The watch-item is whether the recovery is durable or simply the result of a lighter first-quarter sailing mix.
periods.recommendations: Convert the SP-3B sprint lessons into a standing preventive-maintenance route for all shore-power cabinets, starting with SP-2A, SP-3B, SP-4C, and SP-5B. Sustain the 2.9-point rebound by keeping the 48-hour berth lock and adding a monthly exception report to the Port Executive Team. Build a Q2 stress test around the first heavy cruise-and-container overlap week so we know whether the operating model holds under growth conditions.

periods.analysis: Utilization reached 50.9%, up 2.2 points from 48.7%, the best result in this sequence but still yellow because the target is 60%. The improvement reflects real operating traction: preventive maintenance reduced cabinet downtime, the berth lock held through several congested weeks, and Pier 2 crews used the second cable team to capture more cruise call hours. Crossing 50% matters, but Dana would not let us celebrate as if the job is finished; Harborview’s airport-and-seaport economy is expanding, and emissions performance has to scale with it. The watch-item now shifts to the remaining 9.1-point gap, especially vessel classes that are technically eligible but still not consistently connecting.
periods.recommendations: Set a 90-day push to move from 50.9% toward the 60% target by focusing on the top ten eligible non-connecting services and assigning each one a carrier, terminal, and port owner. Extend the second cable-team model through the summer cruise schedule and keep preventive maintenance on a fixed route rather than a trouble-call basis. Bring a tariff incentive or priority-berthing proposal to the Port Commission for vessels that arrive certified and connect within the planned window.

periods.analysis: At-berth shore-power utilization improved from 50.9% to 53.2%, but remains 6.8 percentage points below the 60% target. The gain in current operations sits alongside a below-plan electrification project and its overdue permit milestone.
periods.recommendations: Track eligible vessel connections and equipment availability separately from the capital schedule. Review mitigation-funding opportunities as an external possibility, not an assumed Harborview award or a substitute for permit clearance.
